title: Connection Pools Oversized for Demand or Server Capacity
pattern: A database or external-service connection pool is unbounded or sized beyond measured concurrent demand and the server's resource budget.
why_bad: Idle connections waste file descriptors, kernel buffers, and server-side threads or processes (often 1-10MB each); excess active connections move contention into the server and can degrade throughput, exhaust database RAM, or trigger server-side connection drops [111, 422, 575, 576].
detection: Either (a) a large database/TCP pool (e.g., > 100 connections) is configured for very low traffic without concurrency evidence, or (b) a database pool lacks a maximum cap or exceeds the server's RAM/CPU/connection capacity or is disproportionately larger than the worker thread pool that uses it. The example counts are illustrative, not fixed thresholds.
counterexample: Measured high-concurrency workloads (e.g., microservices serving tens of thousands of concurrent requests per second) with capacity-backed pool sizing; modest, calibrated bounded pools sized to match the maximum number of concurrent request-handling threads.
fix: Measure concurrent connection demand and the server budget, then set a bounded pool with a small idle baseline (e.g., 5 to 10 connections) and an acquisition timeout. Permit growth only within that budget when profiled concurrency justifies it; do not treat an example count as a universal target.
source: *Systems Performance*, Chapter 2 (p. 111); *Release It!*, Section 10 (p. 422); *Pragmatic Programmers - Release It! (Nygard), p. 176, 178 [574, 575, 576]*
